# No One Model to Predict Them All: Extracting Psychosis Symptoms from Clinical Notes using Natural Language Processing. {.tabset}

<br>

**Siobhan K. Lock, Joanne C. Boisson, Lowri M. Evans, Yuefeng Shi, Djenifer B. Kappel, James T.R. Walters, Michael C. O’Donovan, Sophie E. Legge, <a href = "mailto: CamachoColladosJ@cardiff.ac.uk"> José Camacho-Collados </a>, and <a href = "mailto: PardinasA@cardiff.ac.uk"> Antonio .F. Pardiñas </a>**

<br>

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as tools for high-throughput, deep phenotyping of psychiatric traits. Applied to electronic health records, LLMs could in principle extract patient symptoms, risk factors, and treatment history at scale. This could generate valuable insights when combined with increasingly available biological data, such as genomics or neuroimaging. Although proof-of-principle LLM-based symptom extractions have been carried out in some medical conditions, the heterogeneity and multifaceted nature of psychiatric disorders, particularly psychosis, requires extensive domain-specific evaluations. Here, we evaluate 14 general-purpose LLMs for extracting eight schizophrenia symptoms from clinical summaries in a severe mental illness cohort (N = 704). Performance across symptoms was poor to moderate (macro F1 = 0.500 – 0.647), with positive symptoms more accurately extracted than negative symptoms. Few-shot prompting, a common strategy for improving LLM task performance, did not significantly improve these results. Nevertheless, LLM-predicted and gold-standard symptom annotations were comparably related to other clinical variables in regression analyses, indicating that individual-level extraction errors attenuated but did not reverse group-level associations, and did so unevenly across symptom domains. While these results indicate that general-purpose LLMs cannot yet extract psychosis phenotypes from clinical summaries with the reliability required for clinical use, current LLM capabilities might have applications in exploratory research employing large psychiatric cohorts. However, closing the performance gap between positive and negative symptom extractions seems essential groundwork to prevent a systematic bias in any LLM-derived characterisations of psychotic symptoms.

```{r  gold standard}
saps_sans_recode <- saps_sans_recode |>
  pivot_longer(!Study_ID, names_to = "Symptom", values_to = "Rating")

# code binary
ssb <- saps_sans_recode
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 0] <- 0
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 1] <- 0
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 2] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 3] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 4] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 5] <- 1
ssb$code <- "Binary"

# code ratings
ssr <- saps_sans_recode
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 0] <- 0
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 1] <- 0
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 2] <- 1
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 3] <- 1
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 4] <- 2
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 5] <- 2
ssr$code <- "Ratings"

# original scale
sss <- saps_sans_recode
sss$code <- "Scores (Original Scale)"

ssbrs <- rbind(ssb, ssr, sss)

ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Hals_LIFETIME"] <- "Hallucinations"
ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Delusions_LIFETIME"] <- "Delusions"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour_LIFETIME"
] <- "Bizarre Behaviour"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder_LIFETIME"
] <- "PFTD"
ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Alogia_LIFETIME"] <- "Alogia"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality_LIFETIME"
] <- "Anhedonia & Asociality"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Affective_Flattening_LIFETIME"
] <- "Affective Flattening"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Avolition_Apathy_LIFETIME"
] <- "Avolition & Apathy"

ssbrs$Symptom <- factor(
  ssbrs$Symptom,
  levels = c(
    "Hallucinations",
    "Delusions",
    "Bizarre Behaviour",
    "PFTD",
    "Affective Flattening",
    "Alogia",
    "Anhedonia & Asociality",
    "Avolition & Apathy"
  )
)

ssbrs <- na.omit(ssbrs)

df1 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Binary")
df1$Rating[df1$Rating == 0] <- "Absent"
df1$Rating[df1$Rating == 1] <- "Present"
df2 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Ratings")
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 0] <- "Absent"
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 1] <- "Mild"
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 2] <- "Severe"
df3 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Scores (Original Scale)")

ssb_fin <- ssb
ssr_fin <- ssr
sss_fin <- sss
```

## <strong> Methods </strong> 
### Methods
#### Study Design and Sample

Participants were drawn from the Cardiff COGnition in Schizophrenia (CardiffCOGS) cohort (N=1310), a clinical sample of individuals with psychotic spectrum disorders (mainly schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and bipolar disorder) recruited from South Wales and surrounding areas. Individuals were recruited from community adult mental health services, inpatient services, and voluntary services across the UK through advertisements and mental health organisations. Participants completed a clinical research interview based on the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN; Wing et al. 1990). The sample was initially restricted to individuals, with any diagnosis, who had clinical summaries available. These were free-text summaries of psychiatric secondary care notes containing narrative descriptions of the individual's clinical history and presentation. The amount of information available varied between participants and this was summarised by trained psychiatrists or psychologists. Individuals were excluded from analyses if no gold-standard ratings were available for any phenotype (N=12), and a small subset of participants was extracted from the dataset to use their notes for in-context few-shot learning (N=8). The final sample size used for LLM-based symptom extraction comprised `r nrow(saps_sans_recode)` participants (**Figure 1**).
This study follows the MLPsych Guidelines for Reporting Machine Learning Investigations in Neuropsychiatry (GREMLIN; Quinn et al. 2024; **Supplementary Materials**). CardiffCOGS received approval from the South-East Wales Research Ethics Committee (07/WSE03/110), and all participants provided written informed consent. 

<br>

```{r fig 1, fig.align='center', out.height="150%", fig.cap= "Figure 1. Flow chart showing ascertainment of sample size used in model evaluation."}

knitr::include_graphics("C:/Users/siobhan/OneDrive - Cardiff University/phd/PhD/Y3/proj/LLMs/ZWriteup/Figure 1.png")
```


<br>

#### Involvement of people with lived experience
Experiments were designed after engaging a panel of three people with lived experience of severe mental illness who described themselves as casual users of AI. This panel helped shape the study focus and contributed to prioritising the assessed outcomes. 

<br>


#### Outcomes

The eight phenotypes of interest were schizophrenia symptoms selected from the global symptom categories in the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS; Andreasen 1984) and the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS; Andreasen 1989). These included hallucinations, delusions, positive formal thought disorder (PFTD), bizarre behaviour, affective flattening, alogia, anhedonia and asociality, and avolition and apathy (**Supplementary Table 1**). 

In the primary analysis, we extracted a binary variable denoting symptom presence or absence from the clinical summaries. Predicted values were compared to gold-standard Global Lifetime Worst SAPS and SANS scores (Legge et al. 2021). Ratings were completed by trained staff (psychiatrists or psychology graduates) supervised by consultant psychiatrists, as previously described (Legge et al. 2021). Interrater reliability was good across SAPS and SANS items (κ = 0.72 – κ = 0.95). Binarized versions of these ratings, for comparison with LLM-based outputs, were generated as described in **Table 1**. 


```{r Table 1 SAPS SANS Ratings}
t1 <- readxl::read_xlsx(path = "ZWriteup/Tables/Supplementary.xlsx", sheet = "T1")

kbl(
  t1,
  escape = FALSE, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c(
    "SAPS/SANS Score",
    "SAPS/SANS Definition",
    "Binary Task"),
  caption = "Table 1. Conversion between ratings on the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS) and Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS) and the binary scale used in the present work."
) |>
  kable_paper()
```



<br>

#### Model Selection and Testing

We assessed a range of LLMs as described in Table 2; only models with the ‘Thinking’ suffix and the Deepseek-R1 line were explicitly trained for reasoning. To preserve participant privacy and data security, clinical summaries were de-identified, and models were open source and runnable in the secure Isambard AI Phase 2 high-performance computing (HPC) environment. Model selection was guided by past success in extracting psychiatric phenotypes (Frydman-Gani et al. 2025) and by novel releases. LLMs were not fine-tuned; however, the eight case summaries that were used to generate few-shot prompts were excluded from model evaluation for both zero- and few-shot analyses to prevent data leakage.

LLMs were run using Python v3.11.7 (Van Rossum and Drake 2009). For efficiency, we used vllm (Kwon et al. 2023) and loaded models using bitsandbytes (Dettmers et al. 2022a; Dettmers et al. 2022b) for in-flight 4-bit quantisation; pre-quantised models were loaded in 8-bit. Where available, sampling parameters followed recommendations in the HuggingFace model card; where none were provided, default settings were used with the max token length set to 32,768. Inference was run three times per model, with mean evaluation metrics reported. Scripts will be made available upon publication at [git hub repo]. 

For comparison, we also assessed several encoder-only models. Most encoder models had been pre-trained on clinical text and were based on BERT or BERT-like architectures. Briefly, we split our sample into training, validation, and test sets following a 7:2:1 ratio. Following our LLM analysis, we trained each model to predict each symptom from clinical summaries using a binary classifier, optimising hyperparameters with Optuna (Akiba et al. 2019). Model performance was evaluated solely on the test set. Full details are provided in the **Supplementary Methods**.


<br>

```{r Table 2 Models}
t2 <- readxl::read_xlsx(path = "ZWriteup/Tables/Supplementary.xlsx", sheet = "T2")

kbl(
  t2,
  escape = FALSE, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c(
    "Full Model Name",
    "Type",
    "Developer",
    "Number of Parameters"),
  caption = "Table 2. Summary of models evaluated for psychosis phenotype extraction.  LLM = Large Language Model; PLM = Pretrained Language Model."
) |>
  kable_paper()
```


<br>

We tested both zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies. Prompts were developed on a subsample of the CardiffCOGS clinical summaries (N = 50) using *Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct* as the reference model. Several prompts were evaluated under zero- and few-shot conditions, with final prompts selected based on performance across the greatest number of symptoms. For few-shot prompts, examples of symptom presence and absence were selected from clinical vignettes in the Dragon-DATA harmonised resource (Lynham et al. 2023). Symptom definitions used in prompts are provided in **Supplementary Table 1**. 

A total of 5,632 zero-shot prompts (704 participants x 8 symptoms) were fed to each model as described in **Supplementary Table 2**. In the few-shot condition, four brief examples were provided for each symptom alongside the gold-standard rating. Examples were presented as text excerpts containing both present and absent cases, as opposed to complete case summaries. All prompts supplied to the LLMs followed the “system” and “user” format, except for the DeepSeek R1 family of models. In those, all information was included within the “user” prompt, and reasoning was enforced via addition of "<think>\n" before the output, as recommended in the model documentation (DeepSeek-AI 2025). The HuggingFace *apply_chat_templat*e method was used to format prompts for each model. 



<br>

#### Evaluation

Data was analysed in R v4.4.1 via the RStudio IDE (R Core Team 2021). Model output was cleaned where additional text accompanied the desired answer, as commonly seen in reasoning model outputs. Metrics were calculated at the per-symptom level, as described in **Supplementary Table 3**. Given that several symptoms are subject to class imbalance, we included measures that are robust to this issue in our evaluation (e.g., F1, Balanced Accuracy). Models were ranked according to mean macro-average F1 score across symptoms, which determined which LLMs were taken forward for downstream analysis.  

To validate LMM-based predictions, we regressed each of the eight extracted phenotypes from the top-performing model against clinical variables known to be associated to the severity of schizophrenia symptoms (Legge et al. 2020; Cardno et al. 2025). These variables included age at onset, course of disorder, ever using clozapine, ever using depot medications, and lifetime worst scores on the Global Assessment Scale (Endicott et al. 1976). All logistic regression models included sex, age at interview, and schizophrenia diagnosis as covariates. The False Discovery Rate (FDR; Benjamini and Hochberg 1995) was used to correct for multiple comparisons. 

Separately, we used ordinal regression to test whether demographic variables (i.e., age, sex, diagnosis, self-reported ethnicity) or text features (i.e., number of characters in the case summary, summariser group; see **Supplementary Note**) were associated with the number of symptoms correctly predicted by the top-performing LLM. Additionally, and separately for each symptom, we sampled 20 participants where the LLM-based phenotype did not match the gold-standard annotation. Case notes from these participants were used to perform a qualitative error analysis to identify broad error categories occurring in our dataset. 

Finally, selecting three comparable models of different sizes, we tested additional prompts to assess whether few-shot prompting improved performance. Where task performance comparisons were required, McNemar’s test was used to compare misclassification rates, with a False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction for multiplicity.

## <strong> Results </strong> 
### Results

We included `r nrow(saps_sans_recode)` participants in this analysis, of which 90% had a diagnosis of psychosis (**Table 3**).  Clinical summaries were written by 17 different summarisers; in some instances, multiple summarises were involved in the writing of a single case note. The distribution of gold-standard ratings for the eight global symptoms is shown in **Supplementary Figure 1**.

```{r antonios fancy models}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(modelbased)
library(marginaleffects)
library(ggeffects)

#### prepare data ####
metrics_comp <- metrics_comp %>% filter(Symptom != "OVERALL (Macro)")

metrics_comp$dim <- NA
metrics_comp$dim[metrics_comp$Symptom == "Hallucinations" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "Delusions" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "PFTD" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "Bizarre Behaviour"] <- "positive"

metrics_comp$dim[metrics_comp$Symptom == "Alogia" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "Affective Flattening" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "Anhedonia & Asociality" | metrics_comp$Symptom == "Avolition & Apathy"] <- "negative"

metrics_comp$sym <- "All other symptoms"
metrics_comp$sym[metrics_comp$Symptom == "PFTD"] <- "PFTD"

glmm_class <-  glmmTMB(`Macro-Average` ~ dim + (1 | family / model), data=metrics_comp, family=beta_family(link="logit"))
glmm_class_df <- data.frame(coef(summary(glmm_class))$cond)
#plot(predict_response(glmm_class, terms = c("dim"), type = "fixed"))
```

No single model demonstrated optimal performance across all eight schizophrenia symptoms (**Table 4**). Maximum macro-averaged F1 scores were attained primarily by Qwen LLMs, though other models performed at comparable levels (**Figure 2**). A beta generalised linear mixed effect model demonstrated that positive symptoms were associated with higher macro-average F1 scores than negative symptoms (β = `r round(glmm_class_df$Estimate[2],3)`, SE = `r round(glmm_class_df$Std..Error[2],3)`, *p* = `r format_p(glmm_class_df$Pr...z..[2])`), suggesting that models were better able to extract this class of symptoms from the clinical texts. The best performance for symptom extraction was seen for Positive Formal Thought Disorder (PFTD); however, the results for hallucinations and delusions were more consistent across models in terms of achieving relatively high F1 scores. The negative symptoms of anhedonia and asociality, as well as avolition and apathy, showed the poorest performance with no model reaching a macro-average F1 score above 0.6. *Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507-FP8* was the top performing model with mean macro-averaged F1 score of `r round(mean(filter(metrics_comp, model == "Qwen 3 A235B Thinking")$'Macro-Average'), 3)` (SD = `r round(sd(filter(metrics_comp, model == "Qwen 3 A235B Thinking")$'Macro-Average'), 3)`; range = `r round(min(filter(metrics_comp, model == "Qwen 3 A235B Thinking")$'Macro-Average'), 3)` – `r round(max(filter(metrics_comp, model == "Qwen 3 A235B Thinking")$'Macro-Average'), 3)`) across symptoms (**Table 5**). Finally, despite many being pre-trained specifically on clinical text, encoder models were outperformed by LLMs in most tasks. Full results are in **Supplementary Figure 2** and **Supplementary Tables 4 – 21**.

poi <- poi |> dplyr::select(c("Study_ID", "Age_at_Interview", "Sex", "AOO", "FINAL_cloz_ever", "GAS_worst_in_psychotic_episode", "SZ_SZAFFDEP_diag", "schizophrenia_diag", "Number_of_admissions", "Depots", "OPCRIT_90_Course_of_disorder"))

df_val <- left_join(predicted_wide, poi, by = "Study_ID")
df_val$Sex <- as.factor(df_val$Sex)
df_val$FINAL_cloz_ever <- as.factor(df_val$FINAL_cloz_ever)
df_val$SZ_SZAFFDEP_diag <- as.factor(df_val$SZ_SZAFFDEP_diag)
df_val$Depots <- as.factor(df_val$Depots)

df_gs <- left_join(saps_sans_recode, poi, by = "Study_ID")
df_gs$Sex <- as.factor(df_gs$Sex)
df_gs$FINAL_cloz_ever <- as.factor(df_gs$FINAL_cloz_ever)
df_gs$SZ_SZAFFDEP_diag <- as.factor(df_gs$SZ_SZAFFDEP_diag)
df_gs$Depots <- as.factor(df_gs$Depots)

  left_join(s3, by = "Variable") |>
  left_join(s4, by = "Variable")

  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, digits = 3)

sdf$p.x <- ifelse(
  sdf$p.x < 0.05,

)

  sdf$p.x.x
)

  sdf$p.y
)
sdf$p.y.y <- ifelse(

  sdf$p.y.y
)

)
sdf$bf.x.x <- ifelse(

)

s1p <- s1 |>

  pivot_longer(!c(symp, Variable), names_to = "stat", values_to = "value")

  dplyr::select(-ci) |>
  pivot_longer(!c(symp, Variable), names_to = "stat", values_to = "value")
s3p <- s3 |>
  dplyr::select(-ci) |>
  pivot_longer(!c(symp, Variable), names_to = "stat", values_to = "value")
s4p <- s4 |>
  dplyr::select(-ci) |>
  pivot_longer(!c(symp, Variable), names_to = "stat", values_to = "value")

sdf_plot <- rbind(s1p, s2p, s3p, s4p)
sdf_plot_n_llm <- sdf_plot |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c("Variable", "symp"),
    names_from = "stat",
    values_from = "value"
  )

#### Formatting Results for Table ####
s1 <- s1 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s2 <- s2 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s3 <- s3 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s4 <- s4 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)

sdf_n <- s1 |>
  left_join(s2, by = "Variable") |>
  left_join(s3, by = "Variable") |>
  left_join(s4, by = "Variable")

sdf_n <- sdf_n |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, digits = 3)

sdf_n$p.x <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$p.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$p.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$p.x
)
sdf_n$p.x.x <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$p.x.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$p.x.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$p.x.x
)
sdf_n$p.y <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$p.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$p.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$p.y
)
sdf_n$p.y.y <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$p.y.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$p.y.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$p.y.y
)

sdf_n$bf.x <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$bf.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$bf.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$bf.x
)
sdf_n$bf.x.x <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$bf.x.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$bf.x.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$bf.x.x
)
sdf_n$bf.y <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$bf.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$bf.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$bf.y
)
sdf_n$bf.y.y <- ifelse(
  sdf_n$bf.y.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf_n$bf.y.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf_n$bf.y.y
)

sdf_n$Variable <- c(
  "Age of Onset",
  "Disorder Course",
  "Clozapine Use",
  "GAS (Worst in Psychosis)",
  "Depot Use",
  "Sex (F)",
  "Age at Interview",
  "Schizophrenia diagnosis"
)

sdf_neg_llm <- sdf_n
llm5 <- s1
llm6 <- s2
llm7 <- s3
llm8 <- s4

    id_cols = c("Variable", "symp"),
    names_from = "stat",
    values_from = "value"
  )

#### Formatting Results for Table ####

s1 <- s1 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s2 <- s2 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s3 <- s3 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)
s4 <- s4 |> dplyr::select(Variable, OR, ci, p, bf)

sdf <- s1 |>
  left_join(s2, by = "Variable") |>
  left_join(s3, by = "Variable") |>
  left_join(s4, by = "Variable")

sdf <- sdf |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, digits = 3)

sdf$p.x <- ifelse(
  sdf$p.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf$p.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$p.x
)
sdf$p.x.x <- ifelse(
  sdf$p.x.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf$p.x.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$p.x.x
)
sdf$p.y <- ifelse(
  sdf$p.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf$p.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$p.y
)
sdf$p.y.y <- ifelse(
  sdf$p.y.y < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf$p.y.y, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$p.y.y
)

sdf$bf.x <- ifelse(
  sdf$bf.x < 0.05,
  cell_spec(sdf$bf.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$bf.x
)
sdf$bf.x.x <- ifelse(

  cell_spec(sdf$bf.x.x, bold = TRUE),
  sdf$bf.x.x
)
sdf$bf.y <- ifelse(

)
sdf$bf.y.y <- ifelse(

)

  "Depot Use",
  "Sex (F)",

)

    tidy(s4e)$term[2],
    tidy(s4f)$term[2],

    tidy(s4f)$term[4]
  ),

    exp(tidy(s4c)$estimate[2]),
    exp(tidy(s4d)$estimate[2]),
    exp(tidy(s4e)$estimate[2]),
    exp(tidy(s4f)$estimate[2]),
    exp(tidy(s4f)$estimate[3]),
    exp(tidy(s4f)$estimate[4])
  ),
  CI_L = c(
    exp(data.frame(confint(s4a))$X2.5..[2]),
    exp(data.frame(confint(s4b))$X2.5..[2]),
    exp(data.frame(confint(s4c))$X2.5..[2]),
    exp(data.frame(confint(s4d))$X2.5..[2]),
    exp(data.frame(confint(s4e))$X2.5..[2]),

  ),

Logistic regressions identified several associations between LLM-predicted symptoms using the results from *Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507-FP8* (**Figure 3**). The following p-values are corrected for the False Discovery Rate. Lower scores on the Global Assessment Scale, indexing poorer functioning, were associated with the presence of hallucinations (OR = `r round(llm1$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm1$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm1$bf[4])`), delusions (OR = `r round(llm2$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm2$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm2$bf[4])`), positive formal thought disorder (OR = `r round(llm3$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm3$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm3$bf[4])`), bizarre behaviour (OR = `r round(llm4$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm4$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm4$bf[4])`), affective flattening (OR = `r round(llm5$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm5$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm5$bf[4])`), and alogia (OR = `r round(llm6$OR[4], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm6$ci[4]`, p = `r format_p(llm6$bf[4])`). A more severe disorder course was also associated with the presence of hallucinations (OR = `r round(llm1$OR[2], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm1$ci[2]`, p = `r format_p(llm1$bf[2])`) and affective flattening (OR = `r round(llm5$OR[2], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm5$ci[2]`, p = `r format_p(llm5$bf[2])`). 

LMM-predicted symptoms were also strongly associated with medication use. Lifetime depot prescription was associated with bizarre behaviour (OR = `r round(llm4$OR[5], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm4$ci[5]`, p = `r format_p(llm4$bf[5])`). Lifetime clozapine use was also associated with hallucinations (OR = `r round(llm1$OR[3], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm1$ci[3]`, p = `r format_p(llm1$bf[3])`) and delusions (OR = `r round(llm2$OR[3], 3)`, 95% CI = `r llm2$ci[3]`, p = `r format_p(llm2$bf[3])`). Full results for analyses using both LLM-predicted and gold-standard symptom phenotypes are in **Supplementary Tables 22 - 25**.

We analysed errors from *Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507-FP8*, the highest-performing model (mean macro-average F1 score = `r round(mean(filter(metrics_comp, model == "Qwen 3 A235B Thinking")$'Macro-Average'), 3)` ). The median number of correctly predicted symptoms was `r median(all_match$total, na.rm = TRUE)`, and over `r round((nrow(filter(all_match, total < 4))/nrow(all_match))*100, 0)`% of participants had 5 or more symptoms correctly predicted. Log-transformed case note length was significantly associated with the number of correct symptom predictions (β = `r round(m1_res$estimate[2],3)`, SE = `r round(m1_res$std.error[2],3)`, p = `r format_p(m1_res$p.value[2])`), accounting for 11% of variance in task success (Nagelkerke’s R2 = `r round(r2_res$R2[2], 3)`). One summariser group was also associated with prediction accuracy (β = `r round(m1_res$estimate[10],3)`, SE = `r round(m1_res$std.error[10],3)`, p = `r format_p(m1_res$p.value[10])`). Full results are in **Supplementary Table 26**.

s$FNF <- paste0(s$FN, " (", round((s$FN / s$Errors * 100), 1), "%)")

s$Correct <- s$Predictions - s$Errors

)

      "Number"
    )),
    list(sum = sum)
  )

```{r McNemar positive vs negative}
setwd(
  "C:/Users/siobhan/OneDrive - Cardiff University/phd/PhD/Y3/proj/LLMs/1sambard_results/1_zs/qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507-fp8/"
)
data <- read.csv("1_run/cogs_predict_clean.csv")

colnames(data) <- c("Study_ID", "Symptom", "Prompt", "Response", "Prediction")
data$Prediction[data$Prediction == 99] <- NA

predicted_sympt <- data
predicted_sympt[predicted_sympt == ""] <- NA
predicted_sympt <- dplyr::select(predicted_sympt, c("Study_ID", "Symptom", "Prediction"))

alt_sns <- saps_sans_recode

colnames(alt_sns) <- c(
  "Study_ID",
  "Hallucinations",
  "Delusions",
  "Positive Formal Thought Disorder",
  "Bizarre behaviour",
  "Affective flattening",
  "Alogia",
  "Avolition and apathy",
  "Anhedonia and asociality"
)

alt_sns <- alt_sns |>
  pivot_longer(-Study_ID, names_to = "Symptom", values_to = "GS_Prediction")

assess_dims <- left_join(predicted_sympt, alt_sns, by = c("Study_ID", "Symptom"))

assess_dims$match <- ifelse(assess_dims$Prediction == assess_dims$GS_Prediction, 1, 0)

assess_dims_p <- assess_dims %>% filter(Symptom == "Hallucinations" | Symptom == "Delusions" | Symptom == "Positive Formal Thought Disorder" | Symptom == "Bizarre behaviour")

assess_dims_n <- assess_dims %>% filter(Symptom == "Affective flattening" | Symptom == "Alogia" | Symptom == "Avolition and apathy" | Symptom == "Anhedonia and asociality")

m <- matrix(table(assess_dims_p$match, assess_dims_n$match), nrow = 2)

mn <- mcnemar.test(m, correct = F)
```


<br>
<br>

At a per-symptom level, false negatives were consistently more common than false positives, except for hallucinations and PFTD (**Figure 4**). We then examined a subset of 20 errors for each symptom, using the thinking tokens (i.e., verbalisations of the model’s reasoning process) to identify the main reasons underlying incorrect predictions. Based on this we identified six broad classes of errors: hypersensitivity, hyposensitivity, missing information, conflicting information, symptom misattribution, and definition errors (See **Figure 5**; full results in **Supplementary Table 27**). We did not identify any instances of seemingly fabricated responses or confabulations, also known as “hallucinations” in the literature (though this term has been discouraged (Østergaard and Nielbo 2023) and we avoid it here for clarity).

ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 5] <- 1

ssb <- ssb[!is.na(ssb$Rating), ]

ssb$Rating <- factor(ssb$Rating)

saps_sans_lrecoded <- ssb |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = "Study_ID",
    names_from = "Symptom",
    values_from = "Rating"
  )

saps_sans_lrecoded <- left_join(ids, saps_sans_lrecoded, by = "Study_ID")
saps_sans_lrecoded <- saps_sans_lrecoded[
  saps_sans_lrecoded$Study_ID %in% ids$Study_ID,
] |>
  filter(if_any(-Study_ID, ~ !is.na(.)))

sns_lrc <- saps_sans_lrecoded

colnames(saps_sans_lrecoded) <- c(
  "Study_ID",
  "SAPS_Global_Hals",
  "SAPS_Global_Delusions",
  "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder",
  "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour",
  "SANS_Global_Affective_Flattening",
  "SANS_Global_Alogia",
  "SANS_Global_Avolition_Apathy",
  "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality"
)

pre <- saps_sans_recoded_lowri_aligned |>
  pivot_longer(!Study_ID, names_to = "Symptom", values_to = "Rating")

post <- saps_sans_lrecoded |>
  pivot_longer(!Study_ID, names_to = "Symptom", values_to = "Rating")

check <- full_join(pre, post, by = c("Study_ID", "Symptom") )%>% drop_na("Rating.x", "Rating.y")

check$match <- ifelse(check$Rating.x == check$Rating.y, TRUE, FALSE)

res <- data.frame(Symptom = NA, 
                  Total = NA,
                  rcd = NA, 
                  pct = NA)


for (i in 2:length(sns_lrc)){
  r <- sns_lrc[i]
  fp <- saps_sans_recoded_lowri_aligned[i]
  s <- colnames(r)
  rc <- table(r, useNA = "ifany")
  og <- table(fp, useNA = "ifany")
  f <- (rc[[2]]/(rc[[2]] + rc[[1]]))*100
  f <- round(f, 1)
  row <- c(s, og[[1]], rc[[2]], f)
  
  res <- rbind(res, row) %>% na.omit()
}

res$Recoded <- paste0(res$rcd, " (", res$pct, "%) " )

afp <- ratesci::scoreci(98, 156, 41, 145, skew = FALSE)
```


```{r overall lowri comparison}
lmcn <- biglowrimcnemar(
  predicted = predicted_wide, # best predictions used in error analysis
  saps_sans_recode_og = saps_sans_recoded_lowri_aligned, # original saps and sans (but taking only the rows that Lowri recoded per symptom)
  saps_sans_recode_lowri = saps_sans_lrecoded
) # the saps and sans scores that Lowri recoded
```

Missing information was one of the most common error types. Gold standard ratings were based on both clinical interviews and case notes, whereas LLM predictions relied only on case note summaries. This information asymmetry implies models lacked, at least sometimes, the context needed to make a correct rating, leading to the observed excess of false negatives. To investigate this further, we identified false positives (`r nrow(check)` symptom ratings from `r length(unique(check$Study_ID))`  participants) and reclassified them using only case note summaries (**Table 6**). Reclassification was done by authors trained as raters (LME, SEL), with high interrater reliability (κ = 0.8813). When symptom status was assessed solely on case note summaries, nearly half (`r paste0(round(table(check$match, useNA = "ifany")[[1]]/nrow(check)*100, 1), " %")`) of ratings changed, and furthermore, model performance improved significantly when compared against these reclassified ratings (χ2McNemar = `r round(mn$statistic[[1]],0)`, *p* = `r format_p(mn$p.value[[1]])`). The proportion of misclassification was significantly different between the positive symptoms of hallucinations and delusions versus the negative symptoms, with roughly 35% more instances resulting in reclassification in the former than the latter (*p* = `r format_p(afp$pval[2])`). 

<br>

```{r lowri table recoded}
kbl(
  dplyr::select(res, -c(rcd, pct)), row.names = F, 
  escape = FALSE, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c(
    "Symptom",
    "Total Assessed",
    "Total Recoded (%)"),
  caption = "Table 6. Changes in gold-standard symptom classifications after reclassification using solely clinical summary information."
) |>
  kable_paper()

```

```{r overall model mcnemar}

zs_dfs <- rbind(q235_zs, qnext_zs, dsq_zs)
fs_dfs <- rbind(q235_fs, qnext_fs, dsq_fs)
sns_dfs <- rbind(saps_sans_recode, saps_sans_recode, saps_sans_recode)
                 
mnm <- bigmcnemar4mods(predicted_zs = zs_dfs, predicted_fs = fs_dfs, saps_sans_recode = sns_dfs)
```


```{r model mcnemar}
qnext <- bigmcnemar4mods(predicted_zs = qnext_zs, predicted_fs = qnext_fs, saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode)
q235 <- bigmcnemar4mods(predicted_zs = q235_zs, predicted_fs = q235_fs, saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode)
dsq <- bigmcnemar4mods(predicted_zs = dsq_zs, predicted_fs = dsq_fs, saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode)

df <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Deepseek Qwen 32B", "Qwen 3 Next 80B", "Qwen3 235B"),
  x2 = c(round(dsq[[1]], 3), round(qnext[[1]], 3), round(q235[[1]], 3)),
  p = c(round(dsq[[2]], 3), round(qnext[[2]], 3), round(q235[[2]], 3)),
  dir = c(dsq[[3]], qnext[[3]], q235[[3]])
)

df$fdr <- p.adjust(df$p, method = "fdr")

setcolorder(df, c("Model", "x2", "p", "fdr", "dir"))


df |>
  DT::datatable(caption = "McNemar's test comparing Zero- and Few-Shot performance across Models", colnames = c("Model", "McNemar's x2", "p value", "FDR", "Best Prompt"), rownames = FALSE, options = list(lengthChange = FALSE, dom = "t")) |>
  formatRound(c("x2", "p", "fdr"), 3) |>
  formatStyle(
    "p",
    fontWeight = styleInterval(0.05, c("bold", "normal"))
  ) |>
  formatStyle(
    "fdr",
    fontWeight = styleInterval(0.05, c("bold", "normal"))
  )

saps_sans_recode_bin <- saps_sans_recode
```

Across all three models prioritised for this analysis, no improvement was observed with in-context learning:Deepseek-Qwen-32B (χ2 McNemar = `r round(df$x2[1], 3)`, *p* = `r round(df$fdr[1], 3)`), Qwen3-Next-80B (χ2 McNemar = `r round(df$x2[2], 3)`, *p* = `r round(df$fdr[2], 3)`), and Qwen3-235B (χ2 McNemar = `r round(df$x2[3], 3)`, p = `r round(df$fdr[3], 3)`). Full evaluation metrics from the few-shot analysis are shown in **Supplemental Tables 28 – 36**, and per-model per-symptom McNemar’s test results in **Supplementary Table 37**.

<br>

#### Energy Use Calculations

We calculated energy use in Kilowatt-Hours (kWh) over this project, by kWh = power * time.  Energy use in kilowatt hours (kWh) was converted to CO2 emissions by multiplying by the carbon intensity of the UK grid at 233 gCO2/kWh. Power consumption was estimated at 660W, in line with Isambard AI caps for each NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip. We used 37.68 node hours, equivalent to 150.72 GPU hours, to complete the LLM portion of this analysis. Based on the above parameters, this equates to 100 kWh or 23.3 kg CO2.

## <strong> Supplementary Methods </strong> 
### Symptom Extraction using Pretrained Language Models (PLMs)
#### Symptom Extraction using Pretrained Language Models (PLMs)
##### Data Preprocessing

Case note summaries and gold standard labels were loaded using the Hugging Face datasets library. Case note summaries were fed to a model specific AutoTokenizer, converting text data to numeric input IDs and creating an attention mask. Gold standard labels were aligned, and missing values were mapped to -100 to ensure that they are ignored during training. The output for each record is a dictionary containing input IDs, attention masks, and aligned gold-standard labels, which are then batched for training. 

<br>

##### Data Splitting Strategy
Case notes were summarised by over X different individuals to form Case note summaries. Some case notes were summarised by more than one summariser; summariser groups were formed from these. To avoid data leakage, the dataset is split as the “summariser group” level rather than randomly. Scheme 1 (S1) data is kept separate from non-S1 data throughout the split. This means a patient record that appears in the training set will never show up in the validation or test sets. The validation and test sets are split in roughly a 2:1 ratio.

<br>

##### Fine-Tuning

We used Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), including standard models like BERT and RoBERTa as well as clinical domain-specific variants, to make predictions from clinical notes. Over the course of the project, the training framework evolved from a single multi-label classifier into a set of specialised binary classifiers.

<br>

##### Multi-Label Classification.

First, each PLM was trained to predict all clinical symptoms at once. The input text is tokenised and passed through the model encoder, which produces a context-aware representation of the whole document (taken from the [CLS] token). This representation is then passed through a dropout layer and a linear classification head to produce a set of raw output scores (logits), one per label. Optuna (Akiba et al. 2019) was used for automated hyperparameter tuning, running 30 trials to find the best combination of learning rate, batch size, and gradient accumulation steps.

Formally, given an input text sequence $X=(x_1,x_2,…,x_n)$, the sequence is tokenized and passed through the PLM encoder to yield contextualized hidden states. We extract the aggregate document representation $h_polled∈R^d$ (typically derived from the [CLS] token, where d is the hidden dimension size).

To generate predictions for L distinct clinical labels, h_polled^ is passed through a dropout layer and a randomly initialized linear classification head:

$$z=W⋅Dropout(h polled)+b$$

where $W∈R^(L×d)$ and $b∈ R^L$ are the trainable weight matrix and bias, and $z$ represents the raw output logits for all labels.

<br>

##### Binary Classification

To align the methodology with the LLM analysis and to push performance further, we switched to training one independent binary classifier per clinical symptom. The model architecture stays the same, but now the output layer only needs to predict one label at a time. Each model is trained from scratch for its specific symptom, so the learned representations can be more precisely tailored to that particular task.

<br>

##### Handling Long Clinical Documents

Clinical notes are often longer than the 512-token limit that standard models like BERT can handle. Mean-Pooling Chunking was used to handle this. The document is split into up to 8 sequential chunks, each within 512 tokens. Each chunk is processed independently by the model to produce its own logit. These chunk-level logits are then averaged to give a single document-level prediction.

Formally, the document is segmented into K sequential chunks (e.g., K=8), each up to 512 tokens long. Each chunk C_K is independently processed by the PLM to produce a chunk-level logit z_K. The final document-level logit z_finalis obtained via mean-pooling:

$$Z_{final} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} Z_{K} $$
<br>

##### Addressing Class Imbalance
Positive cases for many clinical symptoms are quite rare, which means a standard cross-entropy loss would just push the model to always predict “negative”. To fix this, we replaced the standard loss with a customised Focal Loss.

<br>

##### Model Inference 
During the evaluation phase, the pipeline dynamically loads the corresponding fine-tuned binary model for each specific label. The model processes the unseen test data to output raw logits (z).

To generate the final prediction, the logit is passed through a Sigmoid activation function to map it to a probability score between 0 and 1:

$$P(y=1∨x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$$

Rather than relying on a default 0.5 cut off, we use an optimal threshold (τ) that was dynamically calculated during the validation phase (optimized specifically for the F1-score). The final hard prediction (0 or 1) is made by comparing the probability against this optimal threshold:

$$\binom{pred}{y} = \{1, if P(y = 1 V x) > t\}$$

<br>

##### Model Evaluation
To make sure our results are reliable and that every data point gets evaluated, we ran the pipeline under two complementary experimental setups.

In the first setup, all records from the S1 summarise group were used as the training set. Records from the remaining summarise groups were then split into a validation set and a test set. The model was trained exclusively on S1 data and evaluated on the held-out non-S1 data. In the second setup, the roles were reversed. Records from all non-S1 summarise groups were used as the training set, and the S1 summarise group was used as the validation and test set. 

The final reported results combine the test outputs from both setups. Because each setup uses a different portion of the data as the test set, together they cover all records in the dataset. This means every data point has been evaluated exactly once.

saps_sans_recode <- left_join(ids, saps_sans, by = "Study_ID")

saps_sans_recode <- saps_sans_recode |>
  filter(if_any(-Study_ID, ~ !is.na(.))) |>

    "Study_ID",
    "SAPS_Global_Hals_LIFETIME",
    "SAPS_Global_Delusions_LIFETIME",
    "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder_LIFETIME",
    "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour_LIFETIME",
    "SANS_Global_Affective_Flattening_LIFETIME",
    "SANS_Global_Alogia_LIFETIME",
    "SANS_Global_Avolition_Apathy_LIFETIME",
    "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality_LIFETIME"
  )

colnames(saps_sans_recode) <- c(
  "Study_ID",
  "SAPS_Global_Hals_LIFETIME",
  "SAPS_Global_Delusions_LIFETIME",
  "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder_LIFETIME",
  "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour_LIFETIME",

  "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality_LIFETIME"
)

saps_sans_recode <- saps_sans_recode |>
  pivot_longer(!Study_ID, names_to = "Symptom", values_to = "Rating")

# code binary
ssb <- saps_sans_recode
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 0] <- 0
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 1] <- 0
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 2] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 3] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 4] <- 1
ssb$Rating[ssb$Rating == 5] <- 1
ssb$code <- "Binary"

# code ratings
ssr <- saps_sans_recode
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 0] <- 0
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 1] <- 0
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 2] <- 1
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 3] <- 1
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 4] <- 2
ssr$Rating[ssr$Rating == 5] <- 2
ssr$code <- "Ratings"

# original scale
sss <- saps_sans_recode
sss$code <- "Scores (Original Scale)"

ssbrs <- rbind(ssb, ssr, sss)

ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Hals_LIFETIME"] <- "Hallucinations"
ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Delusions_LIFETIME"] <- "Delusions"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour_LIFETIME"
] <- "Bizarre Behaviour"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder_LIFETIME"
] <- "PFTD"
ssbrs$Symptom[ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Alogia_LIFETIME"] <- "Alogia"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality_LIFETIME"
] <- "Anhedonia & Asociality"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Affective_Flattening_LIFETIME"
] <- "Affective Flattening"
ssbrs$Symptom[
  ssbrs$Symptom == "SANS_Global_Avolition_Apathy_LIFETIME"
] <- "Avolition & Apathy"

ssbrs$Symptom <- factor(
  ssbrs$Symptom,
  levels = c(
    "Hallucinations",
    "Delusions",
    "Bizarre Behaviour",
    "PFTD",
    "Affective Flattening",
    "Alogia",
    "Anhedonia & Asociality",
    "Avolition & Apathy"

)

ssbrs <- na.omit(ssbrs)

df1 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Binary")
df1$Rating[df1$Rating == 0] <- "Absent"
df1$Rating[df1$Rating == 1] <- "Present"
df2 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Ratings")
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 0] <- "Absent"
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 1] <- "Mild"
df2$Rating[df2$Rating == 2] <- "Severe"
df3 <- filter(ssbrs, code == "Scores (Original Scale)")

p1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x = Rating, fill = Symptom)) +

c1 <- sdf_plot_p_llm %>% dplyr::select(c("Variable", "symp", "OR", "bf"))
c1$beta <- log(c1$OR)
c1$class <- "LLM-Predicted"
c1$dim <- "Positive"

c2 <- sdf_plot_n_llm %>% dplyr::select(c("Variable", "symp", "OR",  "bf"))
c2$beta <- log(c2$OR)
c2$class <- "LLM-Predicted"
c2$dim <- "Negative"

c_llm <- rbind(c1,c2)

c3 <- sdf_plot_p %>% dplyr::select(c("Variable", "symp", "OR",  "bf"))
c3$beta <- log(c3$OR)
c3$class <- "Gold-Standard"
c3$dim <- "Positive"

c4$beta <- log(c4$OR)
c4$class <- "Gold-Standard"

c_gs <- rbind(c3,c4)

corrs <- full_join(c_llm, c_gs, by = c("Variable", "symp", "dim"))

corrs$dir <- ifelse(corrs$beta.x * corrs$beta.y > 0, "same", "different")

corrs$sig <- "ignore"
#corrs$sig[corrs$bf.x < 0.05 | corrs$bf.y < 0.05] <- "either"
corrs$sig[corrs$bf.y < 0.05] <- "gs" # "Gold-Standard ONLY (FDR < 0.05)"
corrs$sig[corrs$bf.x < 0.05 & corrs$bf.y < 0.05] <- "both" # "Both (FDR < 0.05)"
# corrs$sig[corrs$bf.x >= 0.05 & corrs$bf.y >= 0.05] <- "Neither (FDR > 0.05)"

cor.res <- cor.test(corrs$beta.x, corrs$beta.y, method = "pearson")

agreed_dir <- nrow(filter(corrs, dir == "same"))/nrow(corrs)*100

res_df <- data.frame(Symptom = NA ,
                     r = NA,
                     p = NA)

symp <- unique(corrs$symp)
for (i in 1:length(symp)){
  s <- symp[i]
  df <- filter(corrs, symp == s)
  r <- cor.test(df$beta.x, df$beta.y, method = "pearson")
  res <- c(s, r$estimate, r$p.value)
  res_df <- rbind(res_df, res)
}

res_df <- drop_na(res_df)

facets <- c("AOO", "GAS_worst_in_psychotic_episode", "Depots1",  "OPCRIT_90_Course_of_disorder" , "FINAL_cloz_ever1")

corrs_f <- corrs %>% filter(Variable %in% facets)

names(corrs_f)[names(corrs_f) == 'beta.x'] <- 'beta.llm'
names(corrs_f)[names(corrs_f) == 'beta.y'] <- 'beta.gs'

p <- filter(corrs_f, dim == "Positive")
n <- filter(corrs_f, dim == "Negative")

#cor.test(y = p$beta.llm, x = p$beta.gs, method = "pearson")
#cor.test(y = n$beta.llm, x = n$beta.gs, method = "pearson")

# y = llm, x = gs

n1 <- lm(beta.llm ~ beta.gs, data = n)
p1 <- lm(beta.llm ~ beta.gs, data = p)

p.i <- p1$coefficients[[1]]
p.s <- p1$coefficients[[2]]
n.i <- n1$coefficients[[1]]
n.s <- n1$coefficients[[2]]

```

    "Bizarre Behaviour",

#### create plot ####
overall_cor_plot <- ggplot(corrs_f, aes(x = beta.gs, y = beta.llm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = dim, fill = dim, shape = sig, size = sig)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = p.i, slope = p.s, colour = "#5E4359", linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_abline(intercept = n.i, slope = n.s, colour = "#A6C7B8", linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.5) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#A6C7B8", "#5E4359"), name = "Symptom Dimension") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#A6C7B8", "#5E4359"), name = "Symptom Dimension") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(ignore = "\u25cf", both = "\u2605",  gs = "\u2795"),
                     breaks = c('both', 'gs'), labels = c("Both \n (FDR < 0.05)", "Gold-Standard ONLY \n (FDR < 0.05)"), name = "Significant Association?") +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(6, 2.5, 3), guide = "none") +
  ylab("log(OR) based on LLM phenotypes") +
  xlab("log(OR) based on Gold Standard phenotypes") +
  xlim(-0.15, 1) + 
  ylim(-0.15, 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotdash") + 
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = c(6,4)))) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = c(4,4)))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#474044", size = 14),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "#474044", size = 11),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "#474044", size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "#474044"),
    plot.title = element_text(colour = "#474044"),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#EFEFEF", colour = "#EFEFEF"), # EFEFEF
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#EFEFEF", colour = "#EFEFEF"),
    legend.text = element_text(colour = "#474044", size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#EFEFEF", colour = "#EFEFEF"),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "#EFEFEF", colour = "#EFEFEF")
  )


overall_cor_plot

##### Supplementary Table 27
###### ST27. Breakdown of Errors
```{r ST27 full error analysis table}
error_res <- error_res_bu_nocol

for (i in 1:ncol(error_res)) {
  error_res[, i] <- paste0(
    error_res[, i],
    " (",
    (error_res[, i] / 20 * 100),
    "%)"
  )
}

error_res_detailed <- t(error_res)


error_res_detailed <- rownames_to_column(
  as.data.frame(error_res_detailed),
  var = "Error"
)
error_res_detailed$Definition <- c(
  "Little, vague, or limited evidence for the symptom in the case note that would not be at an appropriate level for a positive rating.",
  "Evidence for the symptom exists in the case note that the model has not picked up on or discounted.",
  "Evidence exists both for and against the symptom’s presence/absence in the case note, with the model prioritising information leading to the incorrect rating.",
  "There is no evidence in the case note that would support a positive rating being made. This has been correctly identified by the model.",
  "There is evidence for another symptom that is mistakenly taken as evidence for the symptom of interest. Alternatively, a symptom present but its due to the effects of drugs or otherwise rather than psychiatric disorder",
  "Model's reasoning is made on incorrect assumptions about the symptom in question."
)

error_res_detailed |>
  dplyr::select(c(
    "Error",
    "Definition",
    "Hallucinations",
    "Delusions",
    "PFTD",
    "Bizarre Behaviour",
    "Affective Flattening",
    "Alogia",
    "Avolition & Apathy",
    "Anhedonia & Asociality"
  )) |>
  DT::datatable(
    colnames = c(
      "Error",
      "Definition",
      "Hallucinations",
      "Delusions",
      "PFTD",
      "Bizarre Behaviour",
      "Affective Flattening",
      "Alogia",
      "Anhedonia & Asociality",
      "Avolition & Apathy"
    ),
    rownames = FALSE, caption = "Supplementary Table 27. Full breakdown of errors identified in error analysis and their definitions.",
    options = list(pageLength = 6, lengthChange = FALSE, dom = "t")
  )
```

#### Supplementary Tables 28 - 36 LLM (Few-Shot) Results {.tabset}
##### Supplementary Table 28
###### ST28. Overall LLM (Few-Shot) Results

```{r ST28 Overall LLM fs Results}
all_symp_fs_all <- all_symp_fs |>
  dplyr::select(c("Model", "Symptom","Precision", "Recall/Sensitivity", "Specificity", "F1 (present)", "Macro-Average","Accuracy", "BAC", "MCC")) |>
  filter(Symptom != "Positive" & Symptom != "Negative") |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  summarise_at(
    vars(c(
      "Precision",
      "Recall/Sensitivity",
      "Specificity",
      "F1 (present)",
      "Macro-Average",
      "Accuracy",
      "BAC",
      "MCC"
    )),
    list(mean = mean)
  )

colnames(all_symp_fs_all) <- c("Model", "Precision", "Recall/Sensitivity", "Specificity", "F1 (present)", "Macro-Average","Accuracy", "BAC", "MCC")

all_symp_fs_all |>

      "Accuracy",
      "BAC",
      "MCC",

#### Supplementary Table 37
###### ST37. Full Results of McNemar's Test (per model, per symptom)

```{r ST37 Full McNemars Test Results}
mod_comp <- list()

for (i in 2:ncol(predicted_wide)) {
  results <- mcnemar4mods(
    predicted_zs = dsq_zs,
    predicted_fs = dsq_fs,
    saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode_bin,
    col_index = i
  )
  mod_comp[[i - 1]] <- results
}

model_metrics <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, mod_comp))
model_metrics$fdr <- p.adjust(model_metrics$p, method = "fdr")

setcolorder(model_metrics, c("symptom", "mcnemar_x", "p_val", "fdr", "dir"))

model_metrics$Model <- "Deepseek Qwen 32B"
model_metrics_ms <- model_metrics


mod_comp <- list()

for (i in 2:ncol(predicted_wide)) {
  results <- mcnemar4mods(
    predicted_zs = qnext_zs,
    predicted_fs = qnext_fs,
    saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode_bin,
    col_index = i
  )
  mod_comp[[i - 1]] <- results
}

model_metrics <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, mod_comp))
model_metrics$fdr <- p.adjust(model_metrics$p, method = "fdr")

setcolorder(model_metrics, c("symptom", "mcnemar_x", "p_val", "fdr", "dir"))

model_metrics$Model <- "Qwen3 Next 80B"
model_metrics_mg <- model_metrics

mod_comp <- list()

for (i in 2:ncol(predicted_wide)) {
  results <- mcnemar4mods(
    predicted_zs = q235_zs,
    predicted_fs = q235_fs,
    saps_sans_recode = saps_sans_recode_bin,
    col_index = i
  )
  mod_comp[[i - 1]] <- results
}

model_metrics <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, mod_comp))
model_metrics$fdr <- p.adjust(model_metrics$p, method = "fdr")

setcolorder(model_metrics, c("symptom", "mcnemar_x", "p_val", "fdr", "dir"))

model_metrics$Model <- "Qwen3 235B"
model_metrics_q <- model_metrics


model_metrics <- bind_rows(model_metrics_ms, model_metrics_mg, model_metrics_q)

model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SAPS_Global_Hals"
] <- "Hallucinations"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SAPS_Global_Delusions"
] <- "Delusions"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SAPS_Global_Bizarre_Behaviour"
] <- "Bizarre Behaviour"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SAPS_Global_Positive_Thought_Disorder"
] <- "PFTD"
model_metrics$symptom[model_metrics$symptom == "SANS_Global_Alogia"] <- "Alogia"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SANS_Global_Anhedonia_Asociality"
] <- "Anhedonia & Asociality"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SANS_Global_Affective_Flattening"
] <- "Affective Flattening"
model_metrics$symptom[
  model_metrics$symptom == "SANS_Global_Avolition_Apathy"
] <- "Avolition & Apathy"

model_metrics$symptom <- factor(
  model_metrics$symptom,
  levels = c(
    "Hallucinations",
    "Delusions",
    "Bizarre Behaviour",
    "PFTD",
    "Affective Flattening",
    "Alogia",
    "Anhedonia & Asociality",
    "Avolition & Apathy"
  )
)

model_metrics |>
  DT::datatable(
    caption = "Supplementary Table 37. McNemar's test comparing Zero- and Few-Shot performance across Symptoms and Models",
    colnames = c(
      "Symptom",
      "McNemar's x2",
      "p value",
      "FDR p value",
      "Best Prompt",
      "Model"
    ),
    rownames = FALSE
  ) |>
  formatRound(c("mcnemar_x", "p_val", "fdr"), 3) |>
  formatStyle(
    "fdr",
    fontWeight = styleInterval(0.05, c("bold", "normal"))
  ) |>
  formatStyle(
    "p_val",
    fontWeight = styleInterval(0.05, c("bold", "normal"))
  )
```
